signals.title: [Bug]: DashScope tiered pricing uses graduated slices instead of the request-size tier
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing - [x] #30738 concerns string coercion inside DashScope tier data and #21249 concerns missing flat prices during budget enforcement, so neither covers this pricing-model mismatch ### What happened? The DashScope cost calculator applies graduated, income-tax-style slicing to `tiered_pricing`, while Alibaba Model Studio selects one tier from the total input-token count and bills all input and output tokens at that tier's unit prices The proxy budget reservation code already implements the request-size model through `select_tier_for_input`, so reservation estimates and post-response spend accounting also disagree with each other This can materially understate logged spend and weaken budget enforcement for large Qwen requests. Cached input is especially inconsistent because the current calculator tiers the cached-token count independently from zero instead of selecting a rate from the request's total input size Alibaba's current pricing rule is documented here: https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/model-pricing The relevant rule says the unit price is selected by total input tokens in one request and all tokens in that request use the corresponding tier All token counts in the reproduction are synthetic and no provider request is made ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c` 2. Run this script from the repository root ```python from litellm.llms.dashscope.cost_calculator import cost_per_token from litellm.types.utils import Usage from litellm.utils import get_model_info from litellm.litellm_core_utils.llm_cost_calc.tiered_pricing import ( select_tier_for_input, tier_rate, ) model = "qwen-flash" input_tokens = 300_000 output_tokens = 2_000 usage = Usage( prompt_tokens=input_tokens, completion_tokens=output_tokens, total_tokens=input_tokens + output_tokens, ) actual_input, actual_output = cost_per_token(model, usage) model_info = get_model_info( model=model, custom_llm_provider="dashscope", ) tier = select_tier_for_input( model_info["tiered_pricing"], input_tokens, ) expected_input = input_tokens * tier_rate(tier, "input_cost_per_token") expected_output = output_tokens * tier_rate(tier, "output_cost_per_token") print( { "actual_input": actual_input, "actual_output": actual_output, "actual_total": actual_input + actual_output, "request_tier_input": expected_input, "request_tier_output": expected_output, "request_tier_total": expected_input + expected_output, } ) ``` ### Relevant log output ```shell { 'actual_input': 0.023799999999999998, 'actual_output': 0.0007999999999999999, 'actual_total': 0.024599999999999997, 'request_tier_input': 0.075, 'request_tier_output': 0.004, 'request_tier_total': 0.079 } ``` For the current `qwen-flash` map, the two tiers are: ```python [ { "range": [0, 256000], "input_cost_per_token": 5e-08, "output_cost_per_token": 4e-07, }, { "range": [256000, 1000000], "input_cost_per_token": 2.5e-07, "output_cost_per_token": 2e-06, }, ] ``` A 300,000-input-token request selects the second tier. The current result instead charges the first 256,000 input tokens at the lower rate, the remaining 44,000 at the higher rate, and the 2,000 output tokens at the first tier because completion tokens are tiered independently ### Current-code analysis DashScope prompt cost calls `calculate_tiered_cost` separately for text input and cached input https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/llms/dashscope/cost_calculator.py#L45-L68 Completion and reasoning tokens are also passed independently to the graduated helper https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/llms/dashscope/cost_calculator.py#L77-L100 The shared helper explicitly implements graduated slicing https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tiered_pricing.py#L28-L95 The same module separately documents and implements Alibaba's all-or-nothing request-size tier selection https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tiered_pricing.py#L102-L132 Budget reservation uses the request-size selector for both input-only and maximum-cost estimates https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L988-L1003 https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L1044-L1064 ### Suggested correction Select one DashScope tier from total request input tokens before splitting plain, cached, completion, and reasoning tokens Apply that selected tier's matching rate to every token category, including cache-specific and reasoning-specific rates with the existing fallbacks Regression coverage should include exact tier boundaries, input beyond the final tier, mixed plain and cached input, and output token counts that would independently fall into a different tier ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? SDK and Proxy cost tracking ### What LiteLLM version are you on? Commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c` ### Contact details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: Budget reservation is skipped when request cost cannot be estimated
signals.text: ### Summary The optimistic budget reservation path returns without reserving anything when it cannot estimate a positive maximum request cost. This is explicit current behavior, but it leaves configured budgets exposed to concurrent overspend for routes or models whose cost cannot be estimated before dispatch ### Current behavior `litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py` calls `estimate_request_max_cost()` from `reserve_budget_for_request()`. If the model is unknown to the cost map, the request has no token-priced cost fields, or the request is an audio route or an image route the estimator cannot price, the function returns `None`. Note that per-image-priced image generation is estimable: `_estimate_image_generation_cost` reserves `n x per-image cost` for `mode: image_generation` and `image_edit`. Per-pixel and size/quality-tiered image pricing still falls through. `reserve_budget_for_request()` then returns without creating a reservation The source comment describes this as falling back to read-time enforcement. Read-time checks are not an atomic admission decision, so concurrent requests can all observe the same spend before any of their final spend updates are committed The `fail_closed_budget_enforcement` setting does not change this missing-estimate branch because it handles failures while reading or reserving a known counter, not the absence of an estimate ### Reproduction Configure a key, team, or end user with a positive `max_budget`, then route traffic to a model or request shape that has no cost estimate At the unit level, the current branch is observable with an unmapped model: ~~~python from litellm.proxy.spend_tracking.budget_reservation import estimate_request_max_cost assert estimate_request_max_cost( request_body={"model": "unpriced-model", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}, route="/chat/completions", llm_router=None, ) is None ~~~ At the integration level, issue multiple requests concurrently while the durable spend is just below the budget and arrange for the provider or a custom callback to report a nonzero final cost. Because no reservation is created, every request can pass the pre-call check against the same old spend. The final committed spend can exceed the configured budget ### Impact This affects concurrency rather than every single request. A request can still be rejected by a later read-time check, but there is no atomic capacity hold for an unpriced request. The risk is higher for multi-worker deployments and for audio, size/quality-tiered image, custom-provider, and otherwise unmapped model routes ### Expected behavior When a positive budget is configured and the maximum cost cannot be estimated, the proxy should have an explicit safe policy. Options include rejecting the request, reserving a configurable conservative amount, or requiring an operator opt-in to the current read-time-only behavior If the availability-oriented fallback is retained, it should emit a clear metric or warning and document that budget enforcement is non-atomic for the affected route types ### Source - `litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py`, `reserve_budget_for_request` - `litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py`, `estimate_request_max_cost`

signals.title: [Bug]: In-memory spend transactions are lost when the database commit fails
signals.text: ### Summary The default non-Redis spend update path drains its in-memory queues before committing them to the database. If the commit fails, the drained transactions are not restored, so spend updates disappear ### Current behavior The default for `use_redis_transaction_buffer` is `False` `_commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer()` first calls: ~~~python db_spend_update_transactions = await ( self.spend_update_queue .flush_and_get_aggregated_db_spend_update_transactions() ) await self._commit_spend_updates_to_db( db_spend_update_transactions=db_spend_update_transactions, ... ) ~~~ There is no `try/except` that restores the flushed batch when `_commit_spend_updates_to_db()` fails. The daily user, team, organization, end-user, and agent queues are flushed in the same method and are also not restored if their subsequent database update fails Daily tag spend has the same defect in a sibling method. `_commit_daily_tag_spend_to_db()` flushes `daily_tag_spend_update_queue` and then calls `update_daily_tag_spend()` with no restore, so a failure there loses the batch too The Redis-buffered sibling has since been hardened with an `uncommitted` dict and a `restore_transactions_to_redis` call in a `finally`, and `_drain_and_commit_daily_tag_spend_from_redis` got the same treatment. That leaves the default non-Redis path as the only one without any recovery ### Reproduction A focused unit test can inject one transaction and force the commit to fail: ~~~python queue = writer.spend_update_queue await queue.add_update(transaction) with patch.object( writer, "_commit_spend_updates_to_db", new=AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("database unavailable")), ): with pytest.raises(RuntimeError): await writer._commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer( prisma_client=prisma_client, n_retry_times=0, proxy_logging_obj=proxy_logging_obj, ) assert await queue.flush_and_get_aggregated_db_spend_update_transactions() == {} ~~~ The final assertion demonstrates that the failed batch has already been removed and is not available for a later retry. The same test shape can be applied to each daily queue ### Impact A transient database outage, deadlock exhaustion, or process-level failure after the flush can permanently undercount key, user, team, organization, end-user, and daily spend in deployments using the default in-memory path ### Related issue Issue [#33872](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33872) covers the corresponding Redis-buffer loss and also discusses partial cross-entity commits. This report is the separate default in-memory path, where Redis cannot be used to replay the dequeued batch ### Expected behavior Treat a flushed queue batch as in-flight until the database commit succeeds. On failure, restore the exact batch with an idempotency strategy, or use a durable outbox that can be retried without double counting The recovery path should also cover each daily queue and should be exercised by failure-injection tests ### Source - `litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/redis_update_buffer.py`, default setting - `litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py`, `_commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer` - `litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/spend_update_queue.py`

signals.title: [Bug]: Pass-through endpoints from raw config dicts skip centralized common checks
signals.text: ### Summary A pass-through endpoint supplied as a raw dictionary with no `auth` key still requires a valid LiteLLM key, but it silently skips the centralized common checks that an `auth: true` endpoint gets. Three call sites read the same `auth` field with two different defaults This report has been rescoped. It originally claimed such an endpoint was completely unauthenticated. That is not true at HEAD, and I have removed the open-proxy framing. `create_pass_through_route()` puts `user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth = Depends(user_api_key_auth)` in the generated handler's own signature, independent of the route-level `dependencies` list, and `check_api_key_for_custom_headers_or_pass_through_endpoints()` reads `endpoint.get("auth", True) is not True`. Both landed in `148485c2a2`, which closed GHSA-7h34-mmrh-6g58. I verified by registering the raw dict below against a `FastAPI` app: route-level `dependencies` is empty, but the resolved `route.dependant.dependencies` still contains `user_api_key_auth` ### Current behavior `_register_pass_through_endpoint()` accepts either a `PassThroughGenericEndpoint` or a raw dictionary. For a Pydantic object, `model_dump()` materializes the default `auth=True`. For a raw dictionary, the registration code reads the field with no default: ~~~python auth: Final[bool | str | None] = endpoint_data.get("auth") dependencies = None auth_enforced: Final = auth is not None and str(auth).lower() == "true" if auth_enforced: dependencies = [Depends(user_api_key_auth)] if path not in LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes.value: LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes.value.append(path) ~~~ So `auth` omitted from a raw config gives `auth_enforced=False`, and the path is never appended to `LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes`. `_run_centralized_common_checks()` then early-returns for that route, using a third reading of the same field that also has no default: ~~~python if isinstance(endpoint, dict) and endpoint.get("path", "") == route and endpoint.get("auth") is not True: return ~~~ The net effect is a key-authenticated endpoint that never runs model-access checks, key/team/user budget checks, or route guardrails, because the proxy classifies it as an explicitly-unauthenticated forwarder ### Reproduction ~~~yaml general_settings: pass_through_endpoints: - path: /internal/provider target: https://upstream.example.test # auth is omitted ~~~ An unauthenticated call is rejected, which is correct and is the part that changed since this issue was filed: ~~~bash curl -i http://localhost:4000/internal/provider # 401 ~~~ A call with a valid key belonging to a fully exhausted budget succeeds anyway, because the centralized checks were skipped. Compare against the same config with `auth: true`, where the request is rejected on budget ### Impact Model-access restrictions, budget enforcement, and guardrails are silently inert on any pass-through endpoint configured as a raw dict without an explicit `auth: true`. Authentication itself is intact, so this is a policy-enforcement gap rather than an exposure ### Expected behavior Read the field consistently. Either normalize every endpoint through `PassThroughGenericEndpoint` before registration, or default the two remaining raw-dict reads to `True` so all three call sites agree: - `pass_through_endpoints.py`, `_register_pass_through_endpoint`: `endpoint_data.get("auth", True)` - `user_api_key_auth.py`, `_run_centralized_common_checks`: `endpoint.get("auth", True) is not True` `tests/test_litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/test_passthrough_auth_default.py` already covers the authentication default from the GHSA fix, so the new regression only needs to assert that a raw dict without `auth` reaches `_run_centralized_common_checks` Related issues [#32202](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/32202) and [#26399](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/26399) discuss other pass-through security boundaries and do not duplicate this default mismatch ### Source - `litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/pass_through_endpoints.py`, `_register_pass_through_endpoint` - `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, `_run_centralized_common_checks` and `check_api_key_for_custom_headers_or_pass_through_endpoints` - `litellm/proxy/_types.py`, `PassThroughGenericEndpoint.auth`

signals.title: [Security]: Cached proxy-admin keys bypass blocked-key checks
signals.text: ### Summary A cached key whose role is `PROXY_ADMIN` returns from `user_api_key_auth()` before the normal `blocked` check. A stale local cache entry on another worker can therefore continue to authenticate after the key has been blocked in the database ### Current behavior After loading a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth`, the proxy has a privileged early return for proxy-admin keys. That path checks expiration and updates request context, but it does not check `valid_token.blocked` The ordinary non-admin path checks `valid_token.blocked` later `block_key()` updates the database and attempts to delete the key from the local cache and the shared cache. The invalidation is not guaranteed to synchronously remove a stale entry from every worker. A worker that still serves the old cached admin object reaches the privileged early return and never consults the database ### Reproduction Use two proxy workers with a shared database and cache: 1. Authenticate an admin key through worker B so its local cache contains `blocked=False` 2. Block the key through the management API or directly in the database 3. Make another request with the same key through worker B before its local cache refreshes 4. Observe that the request passes the admin early-return path, while a normal key would reach the blocked-key check A focused test can construct a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=PROXY_ADMIN, blocked=False)`, make the shared cache miss or stale, and assert that `user_api_key_auth()` does not authorize the key after an authoritative blocked record is present ### Impact Blocking an admin key is not an immediate revocation guarantee across workers. The stale key can continue to access management and model routes for the cache lifetime or until invalidation succeeds ### Expected behavior Run the blocked-key check before any privileged early return. For proxy-admin keys, either revalidate the blocked state against the database on every request or use a revocation version or generation that can be checked across workers without trusting the stale object Add a multi-worker cache invalidation test that blocks a warmed admin key and verifies the next request is rejected ### Source - `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, cached `PROXY_ADMIN` early return - `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, normal blocked-key check - `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_delete_cache_key_object`

signals.title: [Security]: Responses ID security fails open for raw or ownerless response IDs
signals.text: ### Summary The Responses ID security hook only checks ownership when an ID can be decrypted into an encrypted LiteLLM response ID with nonempty owner metadata. Raw IDs and IDs returned unchanged after encryption setup fails bypass the ownership check, and an encrypted ID with empty user and team fields is accepted for every non-admin key ### Current behavior The pre-call hook calls `check_user_access_to_response_id()` only when `_is_encrypted_response_id()` returns `True`. If decryption fails or the ID is not in the expected managed format, the hook forwards the ID without an ownership check When `LITELLM_SALT_KEY` and `master_key` are both absent, `_encrypt_response_id()` logs at debug level and returns the provider response unchanged. This means a deployment with the security feature enabled can still return a raw response ID and later skip the security hook The encrypted ID includes `user_api_key_dict.user_id or ""` and `team_id or ""`. The checker only rejects when either decoded field is truthy and differs from the caller. If both are empty, the function returns `True` for any non-admin caller ### Reproduction The missing-key path can be exercised with `disable_responses_id_security` left at its default `False`, no `LITELLM_SALT_KEY`, and no `master_key`: 1. Make a successful Responses API request 2. Observe that the response ID is returned in its provider form because `_encrypt_response_id()` skipped encryption 3. Use a different valid LiteLLM key to retrieve, cancel, or list input items for that ID 4. The pre-call hook treats the raw ID as not encrypted and forwards it The ownerless path can be tested directly: ~~~python assert hook.check_user_access_to_response_id( response_id_user_id="", response_id_team_id="", user_api_key_dict=another_valid_key, ) ~~~ The assertion succeeds for a non-admin key even though no ownership relation was established ### Impact A valid LiteLLM key can access another tenant's Responses API object when the provider ID is known or exposed, subject to the provider credential and endpoint behavior. Missing encryption configuration silently downgrades the feature from an ownership check to pass-through behavior The security setting is enabled by default, so missing signing-key configuration should not silently disable its core guarantee ### Expected behavior Fail startup or fail the Responses request when response ID security is enabled but no signing key is available. Every accepted response ID should have a verifiable ownership binding, or the proxy should perform a server-side ownership lookup for raw provider IDs Treat an encrypted ID with no user and no team owner as invalid unless an explicit administrative or system path is being used ### Source - `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, pre-call ID type gate - `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `check_user_access_to_response_id` - `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_encrypt_response_id` - `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_get_signing_key`

signals.title: [Bug]: Project updates leave blocked, model, and budget auth state stale
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing - [x] [#25553](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/25553) is related cache-coherence work for virtual keys but does not cover project objects or `/project/update` ### What happened? The enterprise `POST /project/update` endpoint updates the project row and its budget or object-permission rows, then returns without refreshing or invalidating `project_id:{project_id}` Authentication resolves projects through that cache key first. `_run_project_checks` then trusts the cached `blocked`, `models`, and budget values. A warmed project can therefore continue using its previous authorization state after an admin blocks it, restricts its models, or lowers its budget The stale direction also affects availability. Unblocking a project or widening its model access can continue to reject requests until the management-object cache expires ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Create an enterprise project with `blocked=False` and attach a key 2. Send one LLM request to warm `project_id:{project_id}` 3. Call `POST /project/update` with `blocked=True` 4. Confirm the database row is blocked 5. Send another request before the management-object cache expires 6. Observe that `get_project_object` returns the cached unblocked project and the request is admitted The same sequence can be repeated by replacing `blocked` with a restrictive `models` update or a lower budget ### Expected behavior After every successful project mutation, update or invalidate `project_id:{project_id}` and any cached included budget or permission data before returning Regression coverage should warm the project cache, mutate blocked, models, and budget independently, and assert that the next auth check observes each change ### Relevant code - [Project update returns after the DB write](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/management_endpoints/project_endpoints.py#L650-L681) - [Cache-first project lookup](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py#L4221-L4270) - [Project auth checks](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py#L280-L350) ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.96.0, commit `b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8`

signals.title: [Bug]: New DB deployments are dropped during router upsert when no existing deployment is found
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? Database-backed deployments are dropped from a proxy pod's in-memory router when they are loaded for the first time through `Router.upsert_deployment()` This affects startup and periodic database reloads. Static configuration deployments remain available, while database deployments disappear from model-list endpoints and cannot receive traffic. Model creation can persist the row successfully and then return an internal error because the new deployment is not live in the pod after reload The regression was introduced by commit [300e710bc34](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/300e710bc34). `upsert_deployment()` calls `get_deployment()`, which returns `None` for a deployment that is new to the current router. It then unconditionally passes that value to `_unregister_pre_routing_strategy_for_deployment()`, where `deployment.litellm_params` is dereferenced With `ignore_invalid_deployments=True`, the resulting `AttributeError` is caught and the deployment is silently dropped Expected behavior: a previously unseen database deployment is added to the router, indexed by model ID, and returned by model-list endpoints ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Run the following against a version containing commit `300e710bc34` ```python from litellm import Router from litellm.types.router import Deployment, LiteLLM_Params, ModelInfo router = Router(model_list=[], ignore_invalid_deployments=True) deployment = Deployment( model_name="database-model", litellm_params=LiteLLM_Params(model="openai/gpt-4o"), model_info=ModelInfo(id="database-model-1", db_model=True), ) result = router.upsert_deployment(deployment=deployment) print(result) print(router.get_model_list()) ``` 2. Observe that `result` is `None` and the router model list remains empty 3. Set `ignore_invalid_deployments=False` to observe the underlying `AttributeError` A minimal fix is to call the unregister helper only when `_deployment_on_router is not None` A focused regression test should start with an empty router, upsert a new database deployment, and assert that the deployment is returned, retrievable by model ID, and present in the model list ### Relevant log output ```shell Error upserting deployment database-model (id=database-model-1): 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'litellm_params'. Dropping it and continuing with other deployments ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? `litellm_internal_staging` containing commit `300e710bc34` ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: adaptive_router: one persisted alpha/beta=0 cell bricks the whole router with 500 gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0
signals.text: ### What happened? A model group configured as LiteLLM's native adaptive router returns **HTTP 500 on every request, permanently**, with: ``` gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0 ``` surfacing from `litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks()`. Once it starts it never recovers, including across proxy restarts. Deleting one row from `LiteLLM_AdaptiveRouterState` and restarting fixes it until the condition recurs. The state row responsible: ``` router_name | request_type | model_name | alpha | beta | total_samples sovereign-router | general | gpt-oss-cloud | 1 | 0 | 1 ``` ### Root cause `litellm/router_strategy/adaptive_router/update_queue.py` — the Prisma upsert's `update` branch correctly uses `{"increment": ...}`, but the **`create` branch writes the raw delta as the absolute value**: ```python "alpha": payload["delta_alpha"], "beta": payload["delta_beta"], ``` `adaptive_router.py::_compute_bandit_delta` can legitimately produce `d_alpha = 0.0` or `d_beta = 0.0` (e.g. `d_beta = misalignment + stagnation + disengagement + failure + 0.5*loop`, all zero on a clean satisfied turn). So the **first** flush for a new `(router_name, request_type, model_name)` cell persists a row with the cold-start prior mass dropped entirely — `alpha=1.0, beta=0.0`. On the next proxy start, `adaptive_router.py::load_state_from_db` does: ```python BanditCell(alpha=row.alpha, beta=row.beta) ``` with no validation, **overwriting** the healthy cold-start cell that `initial_cell()` would have produced (`COLD_START_MASS = 10.0`, so alpha ∈ [3, 9.5], beta ∈ [0.5, 7]). `bandit.py:81` then calls `r.betavariate(cell.alpha, cell.beta)`. CPython's `betavariate` delegates to `gammavariate`, which raises `ValueError` when either parameter is ≤ 0. Because `pick_best()` samples **every** eligible model's cell for the classified request type, a single poisoned cell takes down every request of that request type — not just requests that would have routed to that model. Minimal reproduction of the raised error: ```python >>> import random; random.betavariate(1.0, 0.0) ValueError: gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0 ``` ### Notes - `bandit.py` and `update_queue.py` are byte-identical in 1.93.0, 1.93.1, 1.94.1, 1.95.0 and 1.96.0.dev2, so this is not fixed by upgrading. The Auto-Router v2 work in 1.94.0 touches `auto_router/` and `complexity_router/`, not the adaptive bandit. - The failure is silent until it isn't: nothing warns that a persisted cell has non-positive parameters, and the router is bricked for that request type from the next restart onward. ### Suggested fixes (either alone is sufficient; both is better) 1. **`update_queue.py`** — seed the cold-start prior in the `create` branch rather than writing the raw delta, so a new row starts from `initial_cell()` mass plus the delta. 2. **`load_state_from_db` / `BanditCell`** — clamp or reject non-positive `alpha`/`beta` on load (fall back to `initial_cell()` and log), so a bad row can never brick the router. Happy to open a PR for (1) if the maintainers prefer that shape. ### Relevant log output ``` {"message": "litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks() - Error occurred while trying to do fallbacks - gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0\nTraceback (most recent call last):\n File \"/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/router.py\", line 6387, in async_function_with_retries ...", "level": "ERROR"} {"message": "litellm.proxy.proxy_server._handle_llm_api_exception(): Exception occured - gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0", "level": "ERROR", "component": "LiteLLM Proxy", "logger": "common_request_processing.py:765"} ``` ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.93.0 (Docker `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.93.0`); code inspected through 1.96.0.dev2

signals.title: [Bug]: Bedrock GPT-5.6 entries use mode responses and a smaller context than OpenAI/Azure
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Rescoped on 2026-08-16 after re-validating against `litellm_internal_staging` at `973329e986`. The missing long-context pricing is fixed; the metadata mismatch is not The three Bedrock GPT-5.6 entries still declare `"mode": "responses"` and `"supported_endpoints": ["/v1/responses"]`, while the 16 OpenAI and Azure entries for the same models declare `"mode": "chat"` with `["/v1/chat/completions", "/v1/batch", "/v1/responses"]`. `max_input_tokens` is also 1000000 on Bedrock against 1050000 everywhere else ``` bedrock_mantle/openai.gpt-5.6-sol mode=responses max_input_tokens=1000000 endpoints=['/v1/responses'] gpt-5.6-sol mode=chat max_input_tokens=1050000 endpoints=['/v1/chat/completions', '/v1/batch', '/v1/responses'] ``` The practical effect is that these models do not present as chat models on Bedrock, so anything keying off `mode` or `supported_endpoints` (model discovery, the chat-completions surface, UI filtering) treats them differently from the identical model on other providers One caveat for whoever fixes this: the `mode` value is load-bearing, not cosmetic. `mantle_supports_responses` in `litellm/llms/bedrock_mantle/common_utils.py` gates native Responses routing on `/v1/responses` being in `supported_endpoints` or `mode == "responses"`, and `mantle_base_segment` uses the `use_openai_responses_path` flag to put gpt-5.x on the `/openai/v1` base. The chat config's own docstring says that base serves both `/responses` and `/chat/completions`. So the safe change is flipping `mode` to `"chat"` and adding `/v1/chat/completions` to `supported_endpoints` while keeping `/v1/responses` and `use_openai_responses_path`, which preserves the gate Also note the entries live under the `bedrock_mantle/` prefix rather than `bedrock/`, and there is no `bedrock_mantle/openai.gpt-5.6` matching OpenAI's unsuffixed `gpt-5.6` ### What changed since this issue was filed Commit `ef305fe4ab` ([#36698](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/36698)) added the 1M context window and the above-272k tiers to all three Bedrock entries, so the original "no costs above 272k" complaint is resolved. The remaining price delta against base OpenAI is a uniform 1.1x (5.5e-06 vs 5e-06 input on sol, and so on), matching the uplift the `azure/us/*` and `azure/eu/*` entries already use, so I no longer believe the prices themselves are wrong ### Steps to Reproduce N/A ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? _No response_ ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? Re-validated on `litellm_internal_staging` at `973329e986`. Originally filed against v1.96.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: interactions.create() silently drops response_format when routed via litellm_proxy (Gemini)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? When `USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true` (or `litellm.use_litellm_proxy=True`) is set process-wide, `litellm.interactions.create()` for a Gemini model silently loses its `response_format` (JSON schema / mime type constraint) with no error or warning, and the model falls back to free-text output. Root cause, traced through the source: 1. `get_llm_provider()` (`litellm/litellm_core_utils/get_llm_provider_logic.py`) checks `LiteLLMProxyChatConfig._should_use_litellm_proxy_by_default()` **first, unconditionally**, before looking at any explicitly-passed `custom_llm_provider`. With `USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true` set, this forces `custom_llm_provider="litellm_proxy"` for *every* litellm call in the process, including `interactions.create()`. 2. `get_provider_interactions_api_config()` (`litellm/interactions/utils.py`) only recognizes `provider == "gemini"`. For `"litellm_proxy"` it returns `None`. 3. Back in `litellm/interactions/main.py`, when `interactions_api_config is None`, the call **silently bridges to `litellm.responses()`** via `LiteLLMResponsesInteractionsHandler` instead of raising or warning. 4. That bridge's request transform, `transform_interactions_request_to_responses_request()` (`litellm/interactions/litellm_responses_transformation/transformation.py`), maps `system_instruction`, `input`, `tools`, and parts of `generation_config` — but has **no handling for `response_format` at all**. It's dropped entirely, silently. Net effect: a caller who explicitly requested strict JSON-schema output via the Interactions API gets back ordinary free-text (Gemini then wraps its answer in a markdown code fence, as it typically does without an explicit JSON constraint), with no exception and no log line indicating the constraint was dropped. This is especially easy to hit by accident: `USE_LITELLM_PROXY` is a reasonable thing to set globally so that `litellm.responses()`/`litellm.completion()` route through a self-hosted LiteLLM Proxy, but doing so silently breaks the Interactions API for the same process. Confirmed present in every version I checked, `1.82.0` through the current latest `1.96.2` (checked wheel/sdist contents directly) — `litellm/llms/litellm_proxy/interactions/` does not exist in any of them, unlike `litellm/llms/litellm_proxy/{chat,responses,image_generation,image_edit,skills}/` which do. ### Steps to Reproduce ```python import os os.environ["USE_LITELLM_PROXY"] = "true" import litellm response = litellm.interactions.create( model="gemini-3.5-flash", system_instruction="Respond only with JSON matching the schema.", input=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Say hello and give a score of 1."}]}], response_format={ "type": "text", "mime_type": "application/json", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"greeting": {"type": "string"}, "score": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["greeting", "score"], }, }, generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 512}, api_base="http://localhost:4000", # a real LiteLLM Proxy instance api_key="sk-...", # a valid virtual key for that proxy ) ``` Expected: request reaches the proxy's `/interactions`-equivalent handling (or, if unsupported, the fallback should still honor `response_format`), returning clean JSON. Actual: request is silently rerouted to `/responses` with `response_format` dropped; the returned text is unconstrained free text (often markdown-fenced JSON, not raw JSON), and `json.loads()` on it fails intermittently depending on how the model chooses to format its answer. ### Relevant log output ```shell # No warning/error is logged - the drop is completely silent. Confirmed via the local proxy's # access log: with USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true, an interactions.create() call for a Gemini model never # produces a "/interactions" (or equivalent) hit on the proxy - only "/responses" hits appear, # confirming the silent bridge. ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy / Interactions API ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.0 (also reproduced on v1.96.2; confirmed present via source inspection back through v1.82.0) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: budget_limits reset clears Redis before reset_at commits (bypass only with disable_spend_logs)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? Rescoped on 2026-08-16 after re-validating against `litellm_internal_staging` at `973329e986`. The ordering defect is real and unchanged. The budget bypass I originally described does not occur under default configuration, and I have corrected that below The multi-window budget reset path clears each Redis enforcement counter before it persists the window's new `reset_at` in PostgreSQL. `_reset_expired_window` zeroes the in-memory and Redis counter and mutates the local JSON, then returns; `reset_budget_windows` performs the database update afterwards. If that update fails, the database still says the old window is due while Redis reports zero spend for it ```python spend_counter_cache.in_memory_cache.set_cache(key=counter_key, value=0.0) if spend_counter_cache.redis_cache is not None: await spend_counter_cache.redis_cache.async_set_cache( key=counter_key, value=0.0, ) window["reset_at"] = compute_budget_reset_at(...).isoformat() return True ``` Only after that helper returns does `reset_budget_windows` call: ```python await VerificationTokenRepository(self.prisma_client).table.update( where={"token": row["token"]}, data={"budget_limits": windows}, ) ``` The same class documents the required opposite order for ordinary key, user, and team spend counters, in the `_invalidate_spend_counter` and `_reset_budget_common` docstrings, and pins it with `test_reset_does_not_zero_counter_when_db_write_fails`. That test covers only the key, user, and team path, not windows, which is why the inversion survives here Expected behavior is commit first, then clear the enforcement counter only for a window whose `reset_at` advance succeeded, matching what the rest of the class already does ### Why this is not a budget bypass by default `_virtual_key_multi_budget_check` passes `window_start=get_budget_window_start(w)` into `get_current_spend`, and because `window_start is not None` the `is_window` branch consults `_authoritative_floor_spend` on every window check rather than trusting the counter. `SpendCounterReseed.from_db` returns `None` for window counters by design, so it falls through to `window_from_spend_logs`, which re-aggregates the old window from `LiteLLM_SpendLogs`. The database still holds the old due `reset_at`, so `window_start` is the old window's start, the sum comes back at the full amount, `_repair_stale_spend_counter` raises the counter back, and the request is rejected My original claim that the reservation path treats the Redis zero as a warm cache hit is literally true of `_is_spend_counter_cache_warm`, but that only affects reservation seeding, which is never reached because auth has already rejected. That hardening landed in `a8b94b9a87` on 2026-06-18, about two months before I filed this The one configuration where the bypass is real is `disable_spend_logs: true`, or a spend-log retention window shorter than the budget window. `window_from_spend_logs` then returns `0.0` rather than `None`, that zero is treated as a verified authoritative floor, and the still-due window gets a second full budget ### User Flow Before a fix, with spend logs disabled: 1. The user has a key with a `budget_limits` window of `$10/day`, has spent `$10`, and its `reset_at` is due 2. The reset job sets `spend:key:<token>:window:1d` to zero 3. The PostgreSQL update of `budget_limits.reset_at` times out, so the stored window is still due 4. The user sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` for a request costing `$1` 5. Spend logs are disabled, so the authoritative floor reads `0.0` and the request is admitted 6. The user can spend another `$9` in the same still-due window After a fix, in every configuration: 1. The reset job computes the future `reset_at` but the PostgreSQL update times out 2. The counter is left untouched because the commit did not succeed 3. The same request is rejected against the still-exhausted old window 4. After a later successful database update, the counter is cleared for the new window ### Proof the bug occurs Create a key or team whose `budget_limits` JSON contains a due window and whose Redis counter is at its maximum, then make the `budget_limits` update raise. The Redis zero is already written with no compensating action. With `general_settings.disable_spend_logs: true`, the next request against that window is admitted ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? Re-validated on `litellm_internal_staging` at `973329e986`. Originally filed against v1.98.0 at `46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff` ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: MCP auto-execute (require_approval "never") hijacks client-side tool_use from agentic clients like Claude Code, breaking all non-MCP tools with "Error executing tool"
signals.text: ## What happened? A model configured with an MCP tool reference using `require_approval: "never"` (so the proxy auto-executes it server-side) is deployed behind an agentic client that sends its own tools in the same request, such as Claude Code sending Read/Bash/Edit. The auto-execute loop takes over the entire tool_use turn and tries to execute every tool_use block the model emits, including the client's own non-MCP tools. Those tools are not in the MCP server map, so the proxy raises a KeyError that gets swallowed into `Error executing tool: '<tool_name>'` and fed back to the model. The model retries, fails again, and eventually gives up. From the client's perspective all of its native tools (Read, Bash, etc.) are broken for any request routed to that model What I expected: when `require_approval: "never"` is set, the proxy should auto-execute only the MCP tools it injected. A tool_use whose name does not resolve to a known MCP server should be passed through to the client unchanged so the client can execute it locally, the way a normal tool_use turn works when no MCP tool is present ## User Flow Before a fix 1. A user creates a virtual key and a team in the LiteLLM proxy UI, then registers an HTTP MCP server (say `image_understand`) and grants the team access to it 2. The user attaches the MCP tool to a model via the model's LiteLLM Params, e.g. `{"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]}` 3. The user points an agentic client (Claude Code) at `POST /v1/messages` on the proxy, using that model and that virtual key. The client sends its own tools (Read, Bash, Edit, ...) alongside whatever the proxy injects 4. The model decides to call Read on a local file. The proxy's auto-execute loop intercepts that tool_use, fails with `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, and returns the error text to the model instead of handing the tool_use back to the client 5. The model retries with Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, and eventually stops with a message saying the tools are unavailable. The user sees tool call failures and the client's native tooling is dead for that model After a fix 1. Same setup as above: MCP server registered, team granted access, MCP tool attached to the model with `require_approval: "never"` 2. The user points Claude Code at `POST /v1/messages` with that model and key, sending its own tools 3. The model calls Read on a local file. The proxy recognizes Read is not one of its MCP tools, returns the tool_use block to the client in the response, and lets the client execute it locally 4. When the model calls the injected MCP tool (`image_understand`), the proxy auto-executes it server-side as before and feeds the result back 5. Both the client's native tools and the injected MCP tool work in the same turn ## Proof the bug occurs I verified the root cause by reading the current main branch (v1.98.0-dev.2). I was not able to capture a full Claude Code trace against my own proxy in time for this report, so the proof below is the code path plus the user-visible symptom. I can add a full end-to-end curl reproduction if the maintainers want one Config / setup: a model with an MCP tool attached via LiteLLM Params ```json {"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]} ``` Version or commit: v1.98.0-dev.2 on main Commands and their full output The auto-execute loop in `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/messages/mcp_handler.py` extracts every tool_use block without checking whether it belongs to an MCP server ``` # line 38-40 def _extract_tool_use_blocks(response): return tuple(block for block in _get_response_content(response) if block.get("type") == "tool_use") # line 139-158 (abridged) for _ in range(MAX_MCP_TOOL_USE_ITERATIONS): if _get_stop_reason(response) != "tool_use": break tool_use_blocks = _extract_tool_use_blocks(response) if not tool_use_blocks: break tool_results = await LiteLLM_Proxy_MCP_Handler._execute_tool_calls( tool_server_map=tool_server_map, tool_calls=list(tool_use_blocks), ... ) ``` `tool_server_map` is built only from the injected MCP tools (in `_process_mcp_tools_without_openai_transform`). When `_execute_tool_calls` looks up a client-side tool name that is not in that map, it throws KeyError ``` # litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py line 675 server_name = tool_server_map[tool_name] ``` That KeyError is caught by the broad except at line 891-905 and turned into the user-visible error string ``` # line 891-905 (abridged) except Exception as e: ... tool_results.append({ "tool_call_id": tool_call_id, "result": f"Error executing tool: {e}", "name": tool_name, }) ``` So a model emitting `tool_use` for `Read` produces `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, which matches what I observed in the proxy spend logs and what Claude Code surfaced as "tool call failed" The symptom from the agentic client side (Claude Code talking to the proxy over `/v1/messages`): the model attempts Read on a file that exists, gets `Error executing tool: 'Read'` back, tries Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, then tells the user it cannot read files or run commands. A plain curl client that sends no tools of its own works perfectly against the same model, because then every tool_use resolves to an MCP tool. This is why the bug is specific to agentic clients that bring their own tools ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0-dev.2 ## Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: MCP routes return HTTP 500 instead of 401 for missing/malformed Authorization (ProxyException escapes into generic handler)
signals.text: ## What happened? Any MCP gateway route (`/mcp/{server}` or the per-server alias `/{server}/mcp`) called **without a valid `Authorization: Bearer <key>`** returns **HTTP 500** with body `{"error":"MCP request failed","details":""}` instead of **401**. The same request with a valid key returns 200 (or 406 when Accept headers are wrong) — the MCP subprocess itself is healthy. Unauthenticated failures are indistinguishable from real server faults. ## Repro ```bash curl -i -X POST https://<proxy-host>/mcp/<server> \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1}' # → HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error # {"error":"MCP request failed","details":""} ``` Expected: `401 Unauthorized` (log shows `Malformed API Key passed in. Ensure Key has \`Bearer \` prefix.`). ## Root cause (source-verified on 1.84.8) 1. `user_api_key_auth` raises via `UserAPIKeyAuthExceptionHandler._handle_authentication_error` → a **`ProxyException`** (`proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py` ~line 1641). 2. `ProxyException` subclasses `Exception`, **not** `HTTPException` (`proxy/_types.py` line 3600). 3. In `proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py`, `handle_streamable_http_mcp` has: ```python except HTTPException: raise # preserves status codes except Exception as e: # ProxyException lands HERE ... error_response = JSONResponse( status_code=HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, content={"error": "MCP request failed", "details": str(e)}, ) ``` Same pattern in `handle_sse_mcp` (second occurrence ~line 2949). Note the rendered body also has `"details": str(e)` empty because `ProxyException.__str__` doesn't carry the message — so the 500 body carries zero diagnostic info. ## Impact - 5xx alerting fires for what is a 401 (we lost ~35 min triaging a "server outage" that was an unauthenticated client). - MCP clients (incl. discovery/seeders) cannot distinguish auth failure from server error and mis-handle retries. ## Suggested fix Catch `ProxyException` (or the litellm exception base) alongside `HTTPException` in both handlers and re-raise preserving the code, or translate to the proper HTTP status + body. Alternatively render `ProxyException.message`/`param` in the response. ## Env - LiteLLM proxy 1.84.8 (docker, self-hosted) - MCP servers via stdio (config yaml `mcp_servers`), auth = LiteLLM virtual keys Related (same symptom family, different auth path): #29261
signals.author: up-guillaume

signals.title: /v1/messages routes openai/ models with custom api_base to the Responses API; use_chat_completions_api returns empty content
signals.text: ### What happened? For a model configured as `openai/<name>` with a custom `api_base`, `POST /v1/messages` is routed through the **Responses API** instead of chat completions. When the upstream serves `/chat/completions` but not `/responses`, the request fails — even though the same model answers correctly on `/v1/chat/completions` through the same proxy. The documented workarounds for this exact case (`use_chat_completions_api: true`, and the `openai/chat_completions/<model>` model-id form) do not resolve it, and the first one **silently returns an empty response instead of an error**, which is the more damaging of the two behaviours. #### Config (minimal) ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-haiku-4.5 litellm_params: model: openai/claude-haiku-4.5 api_base: https://api.enterprise.githubcopilot.com # serves /chat/completions, not /responses api_key: os.environ/UPSTREAM_API_KEY extra_headers: Copilot-Integration-Id: vscode-chat Editor-Version: vscode/1.99.0 general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY ``` #### 1. Baseline — `/v1/chat/completions` works ```bash curl -s -X POST $PROXY/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"claude-haiku-4.5","max_tokens":16, "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly: CHAT OK"}]}' ``` `HTTP 200` → `CHAT OK` #### 2. `/v1/messages` on the same model — HTTP 400 ```bash curl -s -X POST $PROXY/v1/messages \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"claude-haiku-4.5","max_tokens":16, "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' ``` ```json {"error":{"message":"litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - {\"error\":{\"message\":\"model claude-haiku-4.5 does not support Responses API.\",\"code\":\"unsupported_api_for_model\"}}\n. Received Model Group=claude-haiku-4.5\nAvailable Model Group Fallbacks=None","type":null,"param":null,"code":"400"}} ``` The upstream error names the **Responses API**, so `/v1/messages` is being bridged onto `/responses` rather than `/chat/completions`. #### 3. Workaround A — `use_chat_completions_api: true` → 200 with empty content Adding the flag documented under *“Opt-in bridge for `openai/` models with custom `api_base`”*: ```yaml use_chat_completions_api: true ``` turns the 400 into a `200`, correctly shaped as an Anthropic message, **but with no content**: ``` top-level keys: ['content', 'id', 'model', 'role', 'stop_reason', 'stop_sequence', 'type', 'usage'] type: message | role: assistant | model: claude-haiku-4.5 content: [] stop_reason: end_turn usage: {'input_tokens': 14, 'output_tokens': 6, 'total_tokens': 20} ``` `output_tokens: 6` shows the upstream **did** generate text, but no content block reaches the caller. Identical at `max_tokens` 20, 200 and 1024. A client (Claude Code) sees a successful, blank reply — worse than the original error, because nothing surfaces as a failure. #### 4. Workaround B — `openai/chat_completions/<model>` → 400 ```yaml model: openai/chat_completions/claude-haiku-4.5 ``` ```json {"error":{"message":"litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - {\"error\":{\"message\":\"The requested model is not supported.\",\"code\":\"model_not_supported\"}}"}} ``` The route prefix appears to reach the upstream as part of the model name. ### Expected `POST /v1/messages` for an `openai/`-provider model whose upstream only implements `/chat/completions` should be translated to chat completions and return the generated content as an Anthropic Messages response. Failing that, `use_chat_completions_api: true` should return the content rather than an empty `content: []`. ### Relevant log output ``` litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - {"error":{"message":"model claude-haiku-4.5 does not support Responses API.","code":"unsupported_api_for_model"}} . Received Model Group=claude-haiku-4.5 Available Model Group Fallbacks=None ``` ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? Reproduced on **v1.83.14-stable** and **v1.96.2** (latest release at time of writing). Both behave identically, so this is not fixed by upgrading. ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_
signals.author: dragoshont

signals.title: [Bug]: LiteLLM proxy silently returns understated token counts when Bedrock CountTokens is unsupported for a model
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? `bedrock-runtime`'s `CountTokens` API does not support most current Anthropic models — including **Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5** (full matrix below; of the current line-up only Sonnet 4.6 works). When it rejects a model, the proxy logs a warning and falls through to its local tokenizer. For these models the local tokenizer is badly miscalibrated, so `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` returns a **confidently wrong, much lower number** with a `200 OK` and no indication to the caller that the value is an estimate. Clients that use `count_tokens` for context management (Claude Code / Claude Desktop do) therefore believe they have far more headroom than they do, keep growing the conversation, and eventually get a hard `400 prompt is too long` from the provider — long after any context-compaction threshold should have fired. ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer running Claude Code against the proxy is told their conversation is ~675K tokens when the model actually measures it at ~1.19M, so their client never trims it and the next turn is rejected outright.** 1. They export `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://litellm-domain` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5`, then start a long refactoring session in Claude Code. 2. As the conversation grows, their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...the whole conversation...]}`. 3. It comes back `200 OK` with `{"input_tokens": 675431}` — a plain number, with nothing marking it as an estimate rather than a figure the model itself confirmed. 4. Their client compares 675,431 against the 1,000,000-token window Opus 5 advertises, concludes it is at ~68% capacity, and does not summarise or trim anything. 5. They send the next turn: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "messages": [...the same conversation...]}`. 6. It comes back **`400`** with `{"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error", "message":"...prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum"}}` — the model counted the identical conversation as **1,227,544** tokens, roughly 1.8× the number they were given in step 3. 7. Every retry fails the same way. Nothing they can request from the proxy reports a number anywhere near 1.2M, so from their seat the rejection has no visible cause. 8. If the proxy has `fallbacks` configured, they never see the 400 at all: the turn returns `200` and at `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` that request is listed against **`claude-sonnet-4-6`**, not the `claude-opus-5` they asked for — with the whole conversation re-charged as fresh input, so its cost on that page is roughly 9× the neighbouring turns. **After a (hypothetical) fix: the same call reports a count the model agrees with, so their client trims in time and the turn succeeds on the model they asked for.** 1. They export `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://litellm-domain` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5`, then start a long refactoring session in Claude Code. 2. As the conversation grows, their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...the whole conversation...]}`. 3. It comes back `200 OK` with `{"input_tokens": 1227544}` — matching what the model itself counts. (Equally acceptable from the user's seat: a `4xx` saying the count is unavailable for this model, which at least tells their client not to trust a guess.) 4. Their client compares 1,227,544 against the 1,000,000-token window, sees it is over capacity, and summarises the earlier part of the conversation before sending anything. 5. They send the next turn: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "messages": [...the trimmed conversation...]}`. 6. It comes back **`200 OK`** with `"model": "claude-opus-5"` and a normal `usage` block. 7. The session continues. Trimming happens whenever the reported count approaches the window, so the wall is never hit. 8. At `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` every turn is listed against `claude-opus-5`, at costs consistent with its neighbours. ### Proof the bug occurs ## Steps to reproduce 1. Configure any model whose Bedrock `CountTokens` support is absent — e.g. ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-5 aws_region_name: us-east-1 ``` 2. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...]}` 3. Observe `200 OK` with an `input_tokens` value, and in the proxy log: ``` LiteLLM:ERROR: handler.py:123 - HTTP error in CountTokens handler: Client error '400 Bad Request' for url 'https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/model/anthropic.claude-opus-5/count-tokens' LiteLLM:WARNING: bedrock_token_counter.py:91 - Bedrock CountTokens API error: status=400, message={"message":"The provided model doesn't support counting tokens."} LiteLLM Proxy:WARNING: proxy_server.py:8772 - Provider token counting failed (400): {"message":"The provided model doesn't support counting tokens."}. Falling back to local tokenizer. ``` ## Scope: this affects every current-generation Claude model on Bedrock This is not one edge-case model. Probed directly against `bedrock-runtime` in `us-east-1` (`aws bedrock-runtime count-tokens --model-id <id> --input '{"invokeModel":{"body":"…"}}'`, body containing a valid Anthropic Messages payload with `max_tokens`): | Model ID | Bedrock `CountTokens` | |---|---| | `anthropic.claude-opus-5` | ❌ `ValidationException: The provided model doesn't support counting tokens.` | | `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8` | ❌ same | | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` | ❌ same | | `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` | ❌ same | | `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5` | ❌ `The provided model identifier is invalid.` | | **`anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`** | ✅ **works** — returns `{"inputTokens": 26}` | | `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` | ❌ unsupported — **the geo prefix alone breaks a model that works bare** | So of the current Claude line-up, **only Sonnet 4.6 can be counted on `bedrock-runtime`.** Every other model — including Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, the current defaults — takes the local-tokenizer path on every `count_tokens` call. Two diagnostic notes for whoever picks this up: - A **different** error message (`max_tokens: Field required`) means the model *is* supported and only the request body was wrong. `"doesn't support counting tokens"` is the real rejection, and is what should gate any retry logic. - The proxy already strips the geo/global prefix when building the CountTokens URL (the logged URL is `/model/anthropic.claude-opus-5/count-tokens` for a model configured as `bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-5`), which is correct — passing the prefixed ID through would fail even for Sonnet 4.6. Worth preserving if this code is touched. ## Measured error Identical text throughout. `claude-sonnet-4-6` *is* supported by Bedrock CountTokens, so it gives an authoritative reference count; the target model's true count comes from the provider's own rejection message, which states both the count and the limit. **Tokenizer ratio** — same text, two models: | source | tokens | |---|---| | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` via Bedrock `CountTokens` (authoritative) | 745,753 | | `global.anthropic.claude-opus-5` — from `ValidationException: prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum` | **1,227,544** | | ratio | **1.646×** | **What the proxy reports** — same 400-paragraph sample: | source | tokens | |---|---| | Bedrock `CountTokens` for `claude-sonnet-4-6` (authoritative) | 12,025 | | proxy `count_tokens` for `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 12,025 ✅ exact (provider path used) | | proxy `count_tokens` for `claude-opus-5` | **11,208** ⬅ local tokenizer, 0.93× the sonnet count | | `claude-opus-5` real count (0.93 → 1.646 correction) | **~19,793** | **The proxy understates this model by ~1.77×.** Note the local tokenizer returns *slightly fewer* tokens than the older model's tokenizer, while the target model's real tokenizer produces considerably more — the two errors compound. ## Impact With a 1,000,000-token model limit, the effective ceiling expressed in numbers the proxy reports is about **565K**. A client that compacts at, say, 80% of the advertised window would trigger at 800K reported — i.e. **~1.41M real, which is past the hard limit.** The safety mechanism is unreachable: the request fails before the threshold is ever approached. Observed in production: a long agentic session ran to ~1.19–1.22M real tokens while the client believed it was around 675K, then failed with `prompt is too long`. Requests below the boundary succeeded normally, so the failure is purely a function of size. Two secondary effects worth noting: 1. **Cost.** If `litellm_settings.fallbacks` is configured, the resulting 400 is silently retried on the fallback model. Prompt caches are per-model, so the fallback runs cold and re-reads the entire context at full price. In our case the per-request cost rose roughly 9×, with no error surfaced to the client and — see below — nothing in the logs. 2. **CPU.** Local tokenization of very large contexts is expensive. Repeated `count_tokens` calls over ~150K-token conversations saturated one of two vCPUs on the proxy host, causing an outage: the app stayed internally healthy while throughput collapsed and health checks timed out. ## Reproduction helper Deliberately overshooting is free — a rejected request is not billed, and the error names both the real token count and the limit, which is the only way we found to obtain a ground-truth count for a model Bedrock will not count: ```python import json, boto3 br = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1") br.invoke_model(modelId="global.anthropic.claude-opus-5", body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 16, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "<oversized text>"}]})) # botocore.errorfactory.ValidationException: # prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? 1.96.2 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: Pass-through — upstream-reported cost and tokens are discarded on non-streaming /v1/messages
signals.author: yoni-veksler

signals.title: [Feature]: Let a pass-through target report which model actually served (x-litellm-response-model)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues Searched for pass-through model naming / logged model from response — no duplicate found. Related but distinct: #37105 (reported cost/tokens discarded on non-streaming), which is a bug in the existing header contract; this one asks to extend that contract by one header. ### The Feature Let a pass-through target report **which model actually served**, so the spend row and Usage screen name it: ``` x-litellm-response-model: <model that actually served> ``` read at the same two places `x-litellm-response-cost` / `x-litellm-total-tokens` already are, and applied as `logging_obj.model_call_details["model"]`. Absent header → nothing changes. **Why the existing surfaces cannot cover this.** On a pass-through route the logged model is decided from the request body *before* the request is forwarded (`pass_through_endpoints.py`, `_parsed_body.get("model") or "unknown"`). For an upstream that picks a model per request — a router, an auto-routing gateway, a fallback chain — that name is not what served, and nothing downstream can correct it: spend row, Usage screen and callbacks all show what the client asked for. `upstream_usage_headers.py` already solves the neighbouring problem for exactly this kind of target: *"some pass-through targets invoke several models internally, so LiteLLM cannot price the request from the response body."* The same sentence applies to the model name — if LiteLLM cannot price it from the body, it cannot name it either. ### User Flow **Before — a proxy admin fronting an auto-routing upstream cannot tell which model served** 1. The admin configures a pass-through endpoint `/gateway` to that upstream and restarts the proxy. 2. A developer sends `POST http://litellm-domain/gateway/v1/messages` with `"model": "some-alias"`, streaming. The upstream routes the request internally and answers, reporting its own cost headers. 3. The admin opens `http://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage` and sees the request grouped under `some-alias`. 4. Every request in that view says `some-alias`, whichever model actually served. The admin cannot answer "which models are we actually using, and what does each cost us?" — the data to answer it never reaches the proxy's own logs, even though the upstream knows it. **After — the served model is what the Usage screen groups by** 1. Same configuration. 2. The upstream additionally answers with `x-litellm-response-model: <served model>`. 3. The developer sends the same request. 4. `http://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage` groups that request under the model that served, and `http://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` shows it on the row. Requests that routed elsewhere show their own model, so the breakdown reflects real routing. ### How far you got Measured against `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-latest` with a real proxy in front of a live upstream: - **Response headers don't reach it.** Nothing outside `upstream_usage_headers.py` reads an upstream response header, and that file reads exactly two. - **The response body only half-works.** On non-streaming, the Anthropic pass-through handler does put the body's `model` on the row — but only when the name is one LiteLLM prices, since the write sits inside the `try` around `litellm.completion_cost()`. A model outside the price map raises, the block is skipped, and the row falls back to the request. On streaming that handler never runs, so the body never matters. - **Rewriting the body is also lossy for clients.** Claude Code carries a hardcoded list of known model names; handed an unfamiliar one it drops the session model on resume (measured). So an upstream cannot safely put a routed name in the body it returns. - **Callbacks are blind.** `PassthroughStandardLoggingPayload` carries url, request body, response body and cost — no response headers — so a custom logger cannot recover it either. - **A local patch works.** Wrapping `apply_upstream_reported_usage` to also read the header and set `model_call_details["model"]` makes the served model appear on the row and in Usage, on **both** streaming and non-streaming, against a real upstream. That is the whole change; happy to send it as a PR. One implementation note from that experiment: the model is better parsed and applied **separately** from `UpstreamReportedUsage` rather than added as a field on it. If a model-only response made `has_upstream_reported_usage()` return true, it would short-circuit the `cost_per_request` path in `success_handler.py` and silently zero a configured cost. Questions before we send anything: 1. Is `x-litellm-response-model` the name you want, alongside `x-litellm-response-cost` / `x-litellm-total-tokens`? Happy to use whatever you prefer. 2. Should it set `model_group` as well, or only `model`? 3. Any objection to it applying on both streaming and non-streaming, given cost already does? ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy — pass-through endpoints / spend tracking + logging.
